newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jew and Arab fear each other in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Jew and Arab fear each other in Hebron.

text.p: Arab and Jew in Hebron share at least one thing: each is sure the other wants him dead.
The fear leads to a hair-trigger tension that has made the West Bank town, holy to both Islam and Judaism, one of the toughest problems for Middle East peace negotiators.
Jewish settler Baruch Merzel, leader of the outlawed anti- Arab Kach movement, lives in a heavily fortified enclave of seven Jewish families in the heart of Hebron.
He says no Jew in the town can accept the yet-to-be implemented partial Israeli withdrawal from Hebron that Israel's previous government agreed to a year ago.
And Merzel says he will fight the withdrawal if Israel's new prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, implements it.

"They want to kill us. They want to throw us out of here. And the Jewish tradition says that if someone comes to kill you, you kill him first," Merzel, who has been under house arrest for two years at the Tel Rumeida enclave, told Reuters.

Some 400 Jews live amidst 100,000 Arabs in Hebron. Under the redeployment deal, Israeli troops would remain to guard the settlers. Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation are now negotiating how to implement the partial handover.

Palestinian Hanna Abu Heckal's home falls within the Tel Rumeida enclave. It therefore does not fall into the 80 percent of Hebron to be handed to Palestinian rule under the redeployment plan negotiated between Israel's previous government and the PLO.
"They are the killers and they pretend they are the victims," said her brother, Khaldoun, now a resident of the United States and in Hebron on vacation, said.
"Right now it's like our house is under arrest," Hanna said. "I plead with the world to free our home from this jail. I ask one thing from this peace process -- peace in this house."
Hebron is sacred to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham. It is a flashpoint of violence.

In 1994, a resident of the adjacent Kiryat Arba Jewish settlement, Baruch Goldstein, whose portrait hangs today in Merzel's home, massacred 29 Palestinians kneeling in prayer at al-Ibrahimi mosque, called by Jews the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
The Jews in Hebron see themselves in direct line with the some 60 Jews slaughtered by Arabs in Hebron in 1929.

Aside from the bloodbaths, both sides keep track of their people killed in clashes and ambushes. Jews returned to Hebron briefly after Israel captured the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war and permanently beginning in 1979.

Hanna Abu Heckal, whose home happens to fall where settlers believe the biblical King David's father was buried, lives alongside the settlers in a virtual Israeli army camp. Shacks abutting Abu Heckal's home house Israeli soldiers.

Palestinian visitors cannot drive up to the Abu Heckal home but must park outside the army roadblock at the entrance to Tel Rumeida enclave. Even on foot, Abu Heckal's visitors sometimes are not allowed to pass.
She said settlers had beaten both her father, 70, and her mother, 60. Soldiers, she said, stood by.
Abu Heckal said there was only one solution: the Jews must be moved from Hebron to nearby Kiryat Arba Jewish settlement -- though she'd prefer the Jews weren't around at all.
"Gathering them in their place, which is Kiryat Arba is not the best but it's better," she said.
